claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5 wt% yttrium to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress irradiation-induced Cr-V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
Yttrium will segregate preferentially to grain boundaries in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Grain-boundary-segregated yttrium will reduce the number of heterogeneous nucleation sites available for Cr-V-rich precipitates.
Inhibiting heterogeneous nucleation will preserve the irradiated alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties.
The yttrium addition will preserve the alloy's low irradiation hardening.
The yttrium addition will preserve or improve the alloy's radiation resistance.
Adding approximately 0.5 wt% yttrium will maintain practical bulk manufacturability.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr-V-rich precipitates under irradiation near 8 dpa.
Cr-V-rich precipitate formation in the unmodified alloy is associated with an increase in hardness.
The unmodified alloy typically experiences increased hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
After irradiation, the yttrium-modified alloy will have a statistically significant reduction in Cr-V-rich precipitate volume fraction relative to the unmodified alloy.
After irradiation, the yttrium-modified alloy will have smaller Cr-V-rich precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
After irradiation, the hardness of the yttrium-modified alloy will be similar to or better than that of the original alloy.
The proposed beneficial effect is expected to persist up to 8 dpa.
The proposed beneficial effect is expected within operational temperature ranges relevant to fusion applications.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes preserving the original alloy's low hardening, whereas the initial-state and baseline fields say that the unmodified alloy exhibits an irradiation-associated hardness increase at approximately 8 dpa. This makes the intended hardness baseline internally inconsistent.
